Let $P$ be a probability measure on a measurable observation space $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, and let $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be IID with law $P$; IID means a common law and mutual independence of the whole family ([[def-probability-measure]], [[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]). Let $(\Theta,d)$ be a metric candidate space with its Borel sigma-algebra ([[def-metric-space]], [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). For each $\theta\in\Theta$, let $m_\theta:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable and assume $P|m_\theta|<\infty$. Define
$$P_nm_\theta=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n m_\theta(X_i),\qquad Pm_\theta=\int m_\theta\,dP.$$

A measurable estimator sequence $\hat\theta_n$ into the Borel target $\Theta$ is an **M-estimator** if it maximizes or minimizes $\theta\mapsto P_nm_\theta$; measurability is as in [[def-estimator-sequence-in-iid-experiments]]. It is an exact maximizer when $P_nm_{\hat\theta_n}=\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}P_nm_\theta$, and an $o_P(1)$-approximate maximizer when the finite measurable gap $\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}P_nm_\theta-P_nm_{\hat\theta_n}$ is $o_P(1)$. For minimization use the gap $P_nm_{\hat\theta_n}-\inf_{\theta\in\Theta}P_nm_\theta$. The notation $o_P(1)$ is that of [[def-op-and-little-op-stochastic-bounds]].

The maximizing and minimizing forms are both included; replacing $m_\theta$ by $-m_\theta$ converts one to the other. This definition does not assert that a maximizer exists, nor that the population criterion $Pm_\theta$ has a unique maximizer. Whenever a random candidate is substituted into the empirical or population criterion, assume that evaluation is measurable and finite.

For each positive integer $n$, let $(\Omega_n,\mathcal A_n,P_n)$ be a probability space and let $X_n:\Omega_n\to\mathbb R^d$ be measurable into the Borel sigma-algebra generated by the Euclidean open sets, where $d\ge1$ is fixed and $\mathbb R^d$ has the Euclidean norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]], [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]], [[def-probability-measure]]). The spaces and measures may depend on $n$; no common probability space is required.

Write $X_n=o_P(1)$ if for every $\varepsilon>0$,
$$P_n(\|X_n\|_2>\varepsilon)\longrightarrow0.$$
Write $X_n=O_P(1)$, or say that $(X_n)$ is bounded in probability, if for every $\eta>0$ there is $M>0$ such that
$$\limsup_{n\to\infty}P_n(\|X_n\|_2>M)\le\eta.$$
For real-valued variables on one common probability space, $o_P(1)$ is convergence in probability to zero as defined in [[def-convergence-in-probability]].

The norms and tail probabilities are part of the definition. Independence is not implicit in either notation.

Let $(T_n)$ be an estimator sequence of an estimand $\psi$ with metric target $(\mathcal T,d)$, and fix $\theta\in\Theta$. The sequence is **consistent in probability at $\theta$** if for every $\varepsilon>0$,
$$P_\theta^{\otimes n}\bigl(\{x\in\mathcal X^n:d(T_n(x),\psi(\theta))>\varepsilon\}\bigr)\longrightarrow0.$$

The error event is measurable: by the triangle inequality, $t\mapsto d(t,\psi(\theta))$ is continuous, so its strict superlevel set at $\varepsilon$ is open in the target metric topology and hence Borel; its preimage under $T_n$ is measurable.

The consistency is **pointwise** because $\theta$ is fixed before the limit. It does not assert uniform convergence over $\Theta$ ([[def-estimator-sequence-in-iid-experiments]]).

derivations.claim: Fix $\varepsilon>0$. If $\{\theta:d(\theta,\theta_0)\ge\varepsilon\}$ is empty, the corresponding metric-error event is empty and its probability is zero for every $n$. Otherwise write $\gamma=\gamma_\varepsilon$, which is finite and positive because the nonempty set contains a point with finite population criterion and [A3] bounds its supremum strictly below the finite $M(\theta_0)$. On the event $d(\hat\theta_n,\theta_0)\ge\varepsilon$, separation gives $M(\hat\theta_n)\le M(\theta_0)-\gamma$. The remaining steps treat this nonempty case.

On that event, [A2] gives $M_n(\hat\theta_n)\le M(\theta_0)-\gamma+U_n$ and $M_n(\theta_0)\ge M(\theta_0)-U_n$. The approximate-maximization inequality [A4] also gives $M_n(\hat\theta_n)\ge M_n(\theta_0)-\rho_n$. Combining them yields $\gamma\le2U_n+\rho_n$.

Since $U_n=o_P(1)$ and $\rho_n=o_P(1)$, the probability of $2U_n+\rho_n\ge\gamma$ tends to zero. Step 2.1 therefore gives $P^{\otimes n}\{d(\hat\theta_n,\theta_0)\ge\varepsilon\}\to0$, which implies the strict-error probability in [F3] tends to zero. Thus $\hat\theta_n$ is consistent.

For the minimizing case, set $\widetilde M_n=-M_n$ and $\widetilde M=-M$. By [A5], the separated-minimum condition becomes separated maximization of $\widetilde M$, and $\widetilde M_n(\hat\theta_n)\ge\widetilde M_n(\theta_0)-\sigma_n$. By [A2], $\sup_\theta|\widetilde M_n(\theta)-\widetilde M(\theta)|=U_n=o_P(1)$. Thus the maximizing hypotheses in steps 1.1–3.1 hold for the transformed criterion, proving consistency in the minimizing case as well.

For an exact or approximate global M-estimator, [F1] and [A6] give $M_n(\hat\theta_n)\ge\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}M_n(\theta)-\tau_n$. Since $M_n(\theta_0)\le\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}M_n(\theta)$, this implies $M_n(\hat\theta_n)\ge M_n(\theta_0)-\tau_n$, which is the relative maximization condition [A4] with $\rho_n=\tau_n$. Thus the theorem applies.

derivations.claim: Fix $\varepsilon>0$. If $\{\theta:d(\theta,\theta_0)\ge\varepsilon\}$ is empty, the corresponding metric-error event is empty and its probability is zero for every $n$. Otherwise $b=b_\varepsilon$ is finite and positive: [A3] gives positivity, and any point in this nonempty set has a finite population equation norm by integrability in [A1]. Put $V_n=\sup_\theta\|\Psi_n(\theta)-\Psi(\theta)\|$ and $R_n=\|\Psi_n(\hat\theta_n)\|$. Both are measurable, and $V_n=o_P(1)$ and $R_n=o_P(1)$ by [A2] and [A4]. The remaining steps treat this nonempty case.

On the event $d(\hat\theta_n,\theta_0)\ge\varepsilon$, separation and the triangle inequality give $$b\le\|\Psi(\hat\theta_n)\|\le\|\Psi(\hat\theta_n)-\Psi_n(\hat\theta_n)\|+\|\Psi_n(\hat\theta_n)\|\le V_n+R_n.$$ Thus the metric-error event is contained in $\{V_n+R_n\ge b\}$. This uses the equation error itself, with no representation of the nonlinear quantity $-\|P_n\psi_\theta\|$ as an empirical average of a fixed criterion.

Since $b>0$, the union bound gives $P^{\otimes n}(V_n+R_n\ge b)\le P^{\otimes n}(V_n>b/3)+P^{\otimes n}(R_n>b/3)\to0$ by [F2] and step 1.1. Step 2.1 therefore implies $P^{\otimes n}\{d(\hat\theta_n,\theta_0)\ge\varepsilon\}\to0$, and hence the same holds with strict inequality. Together with the empty case of step 1.1, this proves consistency for every $\varepsilon>0$ by [F4].

A measurable estimator sequence $\hat\theta_n$ into the Borel target $\Theta$ is an **M-estimator** if it maximizes or minimizes $\theta\mapsto P_nm_\theta$; measurability is as in [[def-estimator-sequence-in-iid-experiments]]. The maximizing and minimizing forms are both included; replacing $m_\theta$ by $-m_\theta$ converts one to the other. This definition does not assert that a maximizer exists, nor that the population criterion $Pm_\theta$ has a unique maximizer. Whenever a random candidate is substituted into the empirical or population criterion, assume that evaluation is measurable and finite.

Let $\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be a parametric model on a statistical experiment, and let $\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T$ be an estimand whose target set $\mathcal T$ is equipped with a metric $d$ ([[def-statistical-experiment]], [[def-parametric-statistical-model]], [[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]], [[def-metric-space]]). For $n\ge1$, the IID sample-size-$n$ experiment has sample space $\mathcal X^n$, product sigma-algebra $\mathcal A^{\otimes n}$, and sampling law $P_\theta^{\otimes n}$ at parameter $\theta$ ([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]). The product law is defined recursively from $P_\theta$; each factor is a probability measure and hence sigma-finite, so the finite product theorem supplies its existence, rectangle formula, and uniqueness ([[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]).

A **nonrandomized estimator sequence** of $\psi$ is a sequence of measurable maps, in the sense of [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]],
$$T_n:(\mathcal X^n,\mathcal A^{\otimes n})\to(\mathcal T,\mathcal B(\mathcal T)),\qquad n\ge1,$$
where $\mathcal B(\mathcal T)$ is the sigma-algebra generated by the open sets of the metric $d$, that is, the Borel sigma-algebra of its metric topology ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). Its sampling distribution at $\theta$ and sample size $n$ is the pushforward of $P_\theta^{\otimes n}$ by $T_n$.

This definition fixes IID repeated sampling and data-measurable estimators. It imposes no measurability on the parameter map $\theta\mapsto P_\theta$ or on $\psi$.

Define $d_{\mathbb{R}} : \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ by
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) := |x - y|$ ([[def-abs-value]]). Then:

1. $d_{\mathbb{R}}$ is a metric on $\mathbb{R}$ ([[def-metric-space]]); it is
   called the **usual metric** of $\mathbb{R}$.
2. For $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and $r > 0$ the open ball is the bounded open interval
   ([[def-interval]], [[def-metric-ball]])
   $$B(x,r) = (x-r,\ x+r),$$
   and the closed ball is $\bar B(x,r) = [x-r,\ x+r]$.
3. Consequently $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is open in the metric topology of
   $d_{\mathbb{R}}$ ([[def-metric-topology]]) exactly when for every $x \in U$
   there is $r > 0$ with $(x-r, x+r) \subseteq U$. This topology is called the
   **usual topology** of $\mathbb{R}$.
4. $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$ is not a bounded metric space
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]): no ball contains $\mathbb{R}$, so
   $\operatorname{diam}(\mathbb{R})$ is not defined.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

derivations.claim: Write $\bar x_n=n^{-1}\sum_i x_i$. Expanding both sides gives $\sum_i(x_i-\theta)^2=\sum_i(x_i-\bar x_n)^2+n(\theta-\bar x_n)^2$, because $\sum_i(x_i-\bar x_n)=0$. Thus $P_nm_\theta=P_nm_{\bar x_n}-(\theta-\bar x_n)^2$, which is uniquely maximized at $\bar x_n$.

Let $\mu=PX$. Expanding $X-\theta=(X-\mu)+(\mu-\theta)$ and using $P(X-\mu)=0$ gives $Pm_\theta=-P[(X-\mu)^2]-(\theta-\mu)^2$. The moment assumptions make the mean and centered second moment finite, so this is uniquely maximized at $\mu$.

The IID sequence in [F4] gives the repeated-sampling context. If every coordinate of $x,y\in\mathbb R^n$ differs by less than $\delta$, then $|\bar x_n(x)-\bar x_n(y)|\le n^{-1}\sum_i|x_i-y_i|<\delta$. Hence the sample-mean map is continuous for the product topology. Inverse images of open sets are open, so the map is Borel measurable under [A1]; it is an estimator sequence by [F2] and is an exact M-estimator by [F1] and step 1.1. The target metric is the usual metric in [F3]. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, given, algebra] ∎

This example identifies the finite-sample and population criteria. It does not claim the global uniform-convergence premise on the noncompact set $\mathbb R$; that premise must be checked separately before applying the consistency theorem.

derivations.claim: The IID data context is as in [F4], and the candidate set is a metric space by [F3]. Each order statistic has the finite min-max representation $x_{(j)}=\min_{S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\},\,|S|=j}\max_{i\in S}x_i$: every j-element subset contains a value at least $x_{(j)}$, while the subset of the first j ordered entries has maximum $x_{(j)}$. Coordinate projections are continuous. For finite vectors $a,b$, the maxima differ by at most $\max_i|a_i-b_i|$: each $a_i\le b_i+\delta$ for $\delta=\max_i|a_i-b_i|$, and the reverse inequality follows by swapping $a,b$; minima satisfy the same bound by negating the vectors. Thus finite maxima and minima, each order statistic, and the stated middle-point selection are continuous, hence Borel measurable under [A1]. The selection is an estimator sequence by [F2].

Put $Q(\theta)=\sum_i|x_i-\theta|$. For $n=2k+1$ and $\theta<x_{(k+1)}$, let $\delta=x_{(k+1)}-\theta>0$. Moving to $x_{(k+1)}$ decreases each of the k+1 distances for indices $i\ge k+1$ by exactly $\delta$; each of the other k distances can increase by at most $\delta$ by the triangle inequality. Therefore $Q(x_{(k+1)})-Q(\theta)\le k\delta-(k+1)\delta=-\delta<0$. For $\theta>x_{(k+1)}$, the k+1 distances for indices $i\le k+1$ decrease by $\delta=\theta-x_{(k+1)}$, while each of the other k distances can increase by at most $\delta$, giving the same strict inequality. Thus the odd-sample median uniquely minimizes $Q$.

For $n=2k$ and $\theta\in[x_{(k)},x_{(k+1)}]$, the first k observations lie at or below $\theta$ and the last k lie at or above it, so $Q(\theta)=k\theta-\sum_{i=1}^k x_{(i)}+\sum_{i=k+1}^{2k}x_{(i)}-k\theta$ is constant on this interval. If $\theta<x_{(k)}$, moving to $x_{(k)}$ decreases the k+1 distances for $i\ge k$ by $\delta=x_{(k)}-\theta$, while the other k-1 distances can increase by at most $\delta$; hence $Q(x_{(k)})-Q(\theta)\le(k-1)\delta-(k+1)\delta=-2\delta<0$. If $\theta>x_{(k+1)}$, moving to $x_{(k+1)}$ decreases the k+1 distances for $i\le k+1$ by $\delta=\theta-x_{(k+1)}$, while the other k-1 distances can increase by at most $\delta$, so $Q(x_{(k+1)})-Q(\theta)\le-2\delta<0$. Therefore the interval is exactly the minimizing set of $Q$ and the maximizing set of $P_nm_\theta$ by [F1].

derivations.claim: The population criterion is $M(0)=0$ and $M(1)=EX_1=p>0$, so its unique maximum is $\theta_0=1$. The empirical criteria are $M_n(0)=0$ and $M_n(1)=\bar X_n\ge0$; the displayed selection therefore attains their maximum for every sample. By [F5], the sample space is $\{0,1\}^n$ with its product sigma-algebra. Each singleton vector is a measurable rectangle, and every subset is a finite union of singletons, so every data map is measurable. The estimator is exact by [F1].

Independence and the Bernoulli finite sample law imply that expectations of products of functions of distinct coordinates factor: the joint mass at each $(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in\{0,1\}^n$ is $\prod_iP(X_i=x_i)$, and summing this product over the finite sample space factors. Expanding $(\sum_iY_i)^4$, every term with an index occurring once has expectation zero by $EY_i=0$ and this factorization; the remaining terms are $\sum_iEY_i^4+6\sum_{i<j}EY_i^2EY_j^2\le n+6\binom n2\le3n^2$. For $Z\ge0$ and $t>0$, $t\mathbf1_{\{Z>t\}}\le Z$, so integrating gives $P(Z>t)\le EZ/t$. Applying this to $Z=(\sum_iY_i)^4$ gives $P(|\bar X_n-p|>\varepsilon)\le3/(n^2\varepsilon^4)$.

For fixed $\varepsilon>0$, the bound in step 1.2 is summable in $n$. By the union bound, $P(\bigcup_{n\ge N}\{|\bar X_n-p|>\varepsilon\})\le\sum_{n\ge N}3/(n^2\varepsilon^4)\to0$; hence only finitely many such deviations occur almost surely. Applying this to $\varepsilon=1/j$ for every positive integer $j$ gives $\bar X_n\to p$ almost surely.

For $0<\varepsilon<1$, the metric-error event is $\{\hat\theta_n=0\}=\{\bar X_n=0\}$, which is contained in $\{|\bar X_n-p|>p/2\}$. Step 1.2 bounds its probability by $3/(n^2(p/2)^4)\to0$; for $\varepsilon\ge1$ the error event is empty. Hence $\hat\theta_n$ is consistent by [F3] in the metric of [F4]. Also, since $p>0$, step 2.1 implies that $\hat\theta_n=1$ eventually almost surely, and $\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}|M_n(\theta)-M(\theta)|=|\bar X_n-p|\to0$ almost surely, displaying the finite-class uniform law.

derivations.claim: By [A1] and [F4], every observation equals $0$ almost surely and the sequence is IID. Thus $P_nm_0=P_nm_1=Pm_0=Pm_1=0$ for every $n$. Both parameters are population maximizers, and every data-measurable choice is an exact M-estimator by [F1]. The uniform error is identically zero, but the population maximum is not separated from the other parameter.

Choose the deterministic estimator $\hat\theta_n=1$ for odd $n$ and $\hat\theta_n=0$ for even $n$. For each $n$ it is a constant function of the data, so every inverse image is empty or the full sample space and it is measurable; by step 1.1 it is exact. For the fixed population maximizer $\theta_0=0$ and $\varepsilon=1/2$, $P\{d(\hat\theta_n,\theta_0)>\varepsilon\}$ equals $1$ for odd $n$ and $0$ for even $n$, so the error probability has no zero limit.

This exact M-estimator is not consistent for $\theta_0=0$ by [F2]. Thus the unseparated population maximum does not guarantee consistency, even when the empirical criterion equals its population version exactly.
